answer.cause: GitHub no longer accepts passwords for HTTPS authentication. You need a [personal access token (PAT)](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens) instead of your GitHub password.
answer.explanation: GitHub stopped supporting password authentication for security reasons. Now you must use a personal access token (PAT) as your password when pushing via HTTPS. This is a one-time setup change, not a fix for your repo state.

steps.why: Temporarily stores your credentials to avoid repeated prompts. This is optional but convenient.
Go to [GitHub Personal Access Tokens](https://github.com/settings/tokens) and create a new token with `repo` permissions. Copy the token (do not share it!).
When GitHub prompts for your password, paste the PAT instead of your GitHub password.
Push your changes to GitHub using the PAT.

warnings: Never share your PAT with anyone. Treat it like a password.

If you accidentally commit sensitive data (e.g., passwords, tokens) to your repo, you must rotate those secrets immediately. If the repo is already pushed to GitHub, the data is exposed and cannot be fully removed from GitHub's servers.
If you used your GitHub password before creating a PAT, Git may still cache it. Use `git config --global --unset credential.helper` to clear cached credentials if needed.
